utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, to you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all of those present in court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Redzic. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Redzic. Could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Izet Redzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As we discussed earlier, part of your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing, and we need to deal with the formalities in relation to that submission first. You testified in the Krajisnik case over two days on the 30th and 31st of August, 2004; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've had the opportunity to review the audio recordings of the Krajisnik testimony, and there's one correction you wish to make, and that correction is to the transcript of the 30th of August, 2004, page 5005, line 18, the figure relating to the number of inhabitants in the municipality the Vlasenica currently states 34.817, and you say it should read 33.817; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with that correction can you confirm that it accurately reflects your testimony at the time?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I confirm that it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if you were asked today about the matters that you testified to in the Krajisnik trial, would you provide the same information to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part the same. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender 65 ter 22599, which is the witness' Krajisnik testimony of the 30th and 31st of August, 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with Your Honours' leave, I'll now read a summary of the witness's written evidence. The witness Izet Redzic is an engineer by profession. After the multi-party elections in 1990, Mr. Redzic was appointed president of the Executive Board of the Vlasenica Municipal Assembly. The witness testified that from late 1991, Muslims began to be dismissed from their jobs and by mid-May 1992, all Muslims had been dismissed from their employment. By mid-1991, the witness had become aware of military activities in the Vlasenica area. Paramilitary units were located at Milici, several kilometres from the town of Vlasenica. These troops maltreated and harassed civilians and erected barricades. Beginning around the end of June 1991, military commanders from local units and units in Serbia, as well civilian authorities, including the accused Mr. Karadzic, came to visit the paramilitary troops in Milici. These visits were reported on television and radio. The SDS formed the paramilitary units. The witness became aware through members of the Serb population that the local army and police were distributing weapons to persons of Serb ethnicity. In April 1992, tanks, artillery, and armed vehicles were deployed in Vlasenica. The witness, Mr. Redzic, headed the Muslim delegation in negotiations between the end of March and the 11th of April, 1992, regarding the division of the municipality into Serb and Muslim parts. The Serb delegation was headed by Milenko Stanic [Realtime transcript read in error "Stanisic"], the president of the Vlasenica Municipal Assembly. Stanic consulted with Rajko Dukic, the president of the SDS BiH Executive Board. The Muslim delegation was told to sign an agreement to divide the municipality, and that if the Muslims did not agree to the Serb demands, tanks would attack and the boundaries would be drawn in blood. The witness therefore signed, under duress, an agreement creating the Serb municipality of Vlasenica, the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica and the municipality of Milici. Stanic told the witness that the orders regarding the division of the municipality had come from high up. Mr. Redzic fled Vlasenica on 18 April 1992. He testified that Muslim men, women and children from villages in the Vlasenica municipality were brought to and detained at Susica camp. Women, children, and some elderly men were then transported to Kladanj. Most of the male population remained in the camp. Stanic told the witness that the Muslim men at Susica were to be exchanged for Serbs. The witness later became aware that many of the men detained at Susica were killed. The witness also describes a mass killing in the village of Zaklopaca which occurred on the 16th of May, 1992. Your Honour, that completes the summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, page 3, line 19, Milenko Stanisic should read Milenko Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, were you born on the 19th of January, 1955, in the village of Dzemat in the Vlasenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 19th of January, 1955, the village of Dzemat near Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: At that time I was a Muslim, and right now I'm declaring myself as a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In order to orient the Trial Chamber, can you very briefly tell us where the municipality of Vlasenica is situated within Bosnia and Herzegovina and the names of the neighbouring municipalities?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Vlasenica is in northeastern Bosnia. It is 50 kilometres away from Zvornik and 100 kilometres from Sarajevo. The neighbouring municipalities are Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, Kalesija in part, Sekovici, Kladanj, Han Pijesak, and there's a small border with Rogatica towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could the Prosecutor's microphone please be switched off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, I have a limited number of questions to clarify some matters in relation to your written evidence which is now before the Court. You testified in the Krajisnik trial about the paramilitary units located in Milici and this is at transcript page 5008. You also testified at transcript pages 5012 to 5014 that on several occasions you held meetings with the chief commander of the army and commander of the barracks in Han Pijesak to discuss the paramilitary units and the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence, the TO, and the TO being put under his command. You said that the commander of the barracks was Colonel Milosevic, the same Milosevic who later became the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you said the commander of the army and the commander of the barracks, were you referring to one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The commander of the barracks was Dragoljub Milosevic, precisely if we're talking about Han Pijesak. He was commander of the barracks in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you say Dragoljub Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Or is it Dragomir? I don't know. I know it's Milosevic. And he was commander in Han Pijesak of the regular military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was your first meeting with the then Colonel Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, when the paramilitary brigade in Milici was established, that was the summer of 1991, there was a great deal of tension because of all the things that the Serb units did. In that period of time, all the way up until the aggression, I had contacts with Mr. Milosevic and his deputy Asim Dzambasovic, so that I would get some promises in view of all the problems that the Muslim population was facing at the time. They asked that all of these problems, and that is to say barricades, provocations, shooting at religious facilities, et cetera, they asked me to negotiate and try to resolve that so that these things no longer happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Redzic. I simply asked you when was the first meeting, but you have answered my -- what were going to be my subsequent questions, so we will move on. You also testified about military and civilian leaders visiting the paramilitary brigade, and this is at transcript pages 5016 to 5017. You state that Mr. Karadzic and other key SDS figures and other people in the BH government visited the units and that this was broadcast on television. How often did this happen, these visits?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the accused here knows that every seven days he came to Zvornik, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, and co-operated with his key people from the SDS in preparing the Serb people for a fight so that they would turn against their Muslim neighbours and the few Catholics that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did this happen? What time period, if you recall? Over what time period was this occurring?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part it was from the month of June onwards until the aggression took place and the war started.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned -- you've mentioned twice now up until the aggression and you just mentioned then when the war started. Could you put a -- for the Trial Chamber, what date or month was that?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: If it has to do with Vlasenica, that means that the JNA, according to what people in Vlasenica knew, the Novi Sad Corps came between the 22nd and 23rd of April. They entered Vlasenica, and they said that they liberated Vlasenica from someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you testified that you left the municipality of Vlasenica on the 18th or 19th of April and that's at transcript page 5053, and from there you went via Kladanj to Tuzla; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You stated that you initially kept in contact by telephone with Milenko Stanic and Brano Drakulic re: transporting people out and that's at transcript pages 5057 to 5058. You further testified that you also had contact with people who fled Vlasenica to come to the area where you were residing and that's at transcript pages 5060 to 5062 and that these people told you about the attack on Vlasenica and the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is scheduled incidents B-18.1, B-18.2 and C-25.3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, are you able to explain who or what were the sources of this information?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: As for my contacts and talks with Mr. Stanic and Mr. Brano Drakulic, they lasted all the way up until mid-June while telecommunications were still operating in that period. In the second half of June, there was a total blockade and all telephone communications were cut off, and I could no longer communicate with these persons I mentioned. However, talks continued with people who were coming from Vlasenica through the woods. They provided information as to what was going on within Vlasenica and in the surrounding villages. However, this had to do with ethnic Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you conducting these talks yourself or -- or who were these talks being conducted by?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part we actually had a service in Tuzla. We were given some premises there, and we had people who were in charge of this. Every citizen could come there, and our task was to provide any kind of accommodation to people and to take care of food and so on and so forth. So since people came invariably, all of these citizens, all of these Muslims who came from Vlasenica, from any part of that area, they provided information. They gave statements, rather, as to all the things that they had seen there. All of that was recorded, and there were proper services that kept strict records about the statements that were given.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also described, and this is at transcript page 5104, what happened in the village of Zaklopaca on the 16th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is scheduled incident A 15.2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you said that "83 civilians were killed, amongst them five or six children, 80 per cent were women, the rest were men." Who or what was the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, when this happened as soon as the aggression broke out on the 16th of May as you said, 1992, it is true that this many people were killed. These people had not been armed. They were civilians, and at the time some Muslims were still coming in. It is important to mention that on the 15th of May, in the bauxite mine, and that was the biggest work organisation there, it accounted for 80 per cent of the economy of Vlasenica, all Muslims were banned from that work organisation. They were not allowed to come there any more. After that these mass killings, executions, took place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. My question was: Do you recall what the source -- who the sources or -- sources or sources were that informed you about the events that happened in Zaklopaca? You mentioned -- sorry, you mentioned that people were coming, but do you recall specifically who in relation to that incident?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: At the time it could be seen on Serb television too. Serb television said that a certain number of people lost their lives there. They said something that was not true, namely that these persons had been armed. I spoke about Stanic at the time, about what was going on in Zaklopaca. I said to him do you see what is happening in Zaklopaca and he quite simply said no one can rule anyone else. These people who fled from Zaklopaca and the neighbouring villages, they were saying about what had happened, how many people were killed, et cetera. There are witnesses who are survivors who were in the woods there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Redzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That finishes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you are minded to tender the associate exhibit of this witness's transcript. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of the two associated exhibits, the first one listed on the notification filed on the 7th July 2011 is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit the 65 ter number 11468.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that is simply an authentication sheet of the five recorded intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would ask what the point is of admitting the authentication sheet when the intercepts are not being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the intercepts Mr. Krajisnik [sic] asked to be admitted yesterday or asked to be MFI'd and that was MFI D1643 which is or was 65 ter number 30186. So in that regard, Mr. Redzic listened to the audio of that intercept and confirmed the speakers. One of them was Mr. Bajagic and the other was Mr. Karadzic. So for that reason the authentication sheet is of some benefit to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So at this moment you're not minded to tender those intercepts themselves. So whatever probative value they may have you are now tendering the authentication by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In his transcript -- in his Krajisnik transcript, he gave evidence that he had listened to the five intercepts and that he recognised the voice of Mr. Bajagic and.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bajagic, Bojagic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's incorrectly spelled in yesterday's transcript but it's B-a-j-a-g-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Zvonko Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes and that's at page 5076 and 5077 of the Krajisnik transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That exhibit can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- we are going to give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P3190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we can seek to tender them at a later stage through another witness who will authenticate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Redzic's authentication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now your examination-in-chief is over, Mr. Redzic. You will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Excellencies; good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Redzic.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I have already said good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, with all due respect, I would like to know whether it is the case that even now when the Prosecutor exhibited the transcript of two days of testimony by this witness and the testimony was provided in a case that resulted in a conviction, can I still manage to challenge all of that within only an hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As is the usual practice, we'll see how you proceed with your cross-examination. Please get on with your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but I have to say that getting such a short time, I make mistakes in haste, and that's a vicious circle that handicaps my defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And also bear it in mind that we admitted entire testimony, which includes the cross-examination, which means you don't have to repeat what was asked before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have said, and it's a fact, isn't it, that the Municipal Assembly of Vlasenica had 60 deputies, including 26 from the SDA, 27 from the SDS, and 7 from the united opposition; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 901127 is the document I would like displayed in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 901127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be some mistake in number, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your indulgence, I'll check now. 1D4054. It's the same subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Would you please see this is the outcome of the elections broken down by local communes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page. Page 3, please. That's the summary of the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the final outcome of the elections including the number of votes and percentages added in hand? Can you see this Serbian version. 21.986 people voted. And then rubric 4 is SDS, rubric 5 is the opposition. Column 7 is the SDA, and 8 are the reformist forces and I don't know who else. Can you hear me, Mr. Redzic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I can hear you, but I didn't understand you were addressing me. The results are correct. That's as I said. There were 60 deputies before the outbreak of the aggression, 27 of the SDS; 26, the SDA; and 7, the opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, since we don't have enough time, whenever we can do without a broader explanation, please answer with a yes or no. You said in your earlier evidence, and you said that in your statement in October, 12 October 1994, on page 00184597, is that the elections reflected, in fact, the ethnic composition of the municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: It's correct. At that time there were two political parties, two political movements, in fact, that had not established themselves yet as political parties, and there were some opposition that was manipulated by the SDS, because there was no way the Serbs would have gotten this number of votes if the ethnic composition had been observed, because the ethnic composition was not honoured, and you can see that from the fact that the entire opposition are Muslims. That's a simple explanation, because the Serbs, according to the percentages, the Serbs could have gotten only 24 seats. All the rest are Muslims including perhaps 1 per cent of Yugoslavs and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that you would be right on the condition that the polling had been accurate and honourable?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The census, you mean, was done very accurately and very honestly because it was conducted by absolutely impartial people representing Serbs and Muslims and every other community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbs objected that the census had been falsified and that's why it never passed verification in parliament?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: If anyone would have known that, I would have known that, because I was a leader among these people, Serbs and Muslims and all the others. I never heard of any such thing, nor was I told of -- of that by -- by any Serb or Muslim representative. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that the census was not ratified in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I simply don't believe that these results had not been accepted. Perhaps maybe if the problems had already occurred, but I don't believe it. This is pure statistics, and for statistics there is a particular institution in charge. It's a different matter if the SDS did not accept it, because they were working against the system, against the country to break up everything that makes up Bosnia and its people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that the answer to my previous question was not recorded in its entirety, so I'm asking you to speak slowly and answer more briefly. Answer only to the point. If we get more time, I'll be able to ask you more about it.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were the president of the Executive Board while Mr. Milenko Stanic from the victorious party was the president of the Municipal Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that Mr. Stanic did not have direct control over the Secretariat for National Defence. Was Milenko Stanic the president of the National Defence council or was it you?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Under the law and under the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the National Defence Council is made up of the president of the Assembly, the president of the Executive Board, the secretary for national defence, the commander of the Territorial Defence, the chief of the MUP, and presidents of the deputies' clubs from the Assembly of Vlasenica. That is the truth, and that is prescribed by law. And it's not designated by name who was a member. It's not a problem if it's Milenko Stanic but it is a problem if there is aggression from outside. In this situation, the Serbs and the SDS took another path as you directed them. That's why the council was never able to properly discharge its functions and play its part. And they would not convene, although I tried very hard to get people together but without any success. I don't have to explain to you what instructions you gave to the Serbian people what they were to do, how to form Serbian Assemblies, Serbian municipalities. You know it all, Karadzic, as well as I know it or anyone here in the courtroom and outside this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you, Mr. Redzic, you are not charged with anything or accused of anything, and I'm not attacking you. I'm just looking for the truth together with you. I'm just asking you were you the president of the National Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I explained a moment ago of whom the National Defence Council is made up of, and at that time the Serbian people from the SDS made themselves available completely at -- to Karadzic and his legions. Nobody was interested any more in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, the National Defence Council did not exist at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your answer was that the National Defence Council did not exist at the time. If the question is a simple one to which you can say yes or no, please do so, because we have only limited time, Mr. Redzic. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your evidence in the Krajisnik case on the 30th and 31st of August, 2004, on page 5012 you said, and I'm going to read it in English now, I hope it's going to be interpreted to you correctly. "[In English][Previous translation continues] ... According to the law and constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Territorial Defence and civilian protection are under the authority of the civilian authorities, and it could be mobilised in the case of natural disaster or other circumstances, storm, large-scale fires, and also the case of war." [Interpretation] Was the Bosnian constitution and the Bosnian Law on National Defence different from the federal law or was it identical?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Of course the republic had to harmonise their legislation and their constitutions to the federal state, but in that period, Yugoslavia was breaking up. Republics were seceding, and many laws were adopted here at conferences in The Hague according to declarations and other documents. Former federal laws were no longer applied in Croatia and Slovenia and they were temporarily continuing to be applied in other republics pending a solution that was to be found as the best solution for everyone, all the peoples in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, let us stick to Vlasenica. You say that in Vlasenica there occurred a legal vacuum, and the laws and the constitution of Yugoslavia were no longer applied. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: When the aggression broke out in the Republic of Croatia. From that moment on, Serbian forces led by the SDS were fighting in every possible way to make federal laws null and void and to apply instead the laws of the Greater Serbia or some other common state they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Redzic, it's not up to you or to me to talk about it today. Let's talk about Vlasenica. How did it come about that you became the president of the National Defence Council when according to the law it should have been Mr. Stanic? And when were federal laws and the constitution suspended in Vlasenica? You were in a position of power.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask the gentleman who's asking me these questions to refrain from comment. I am prepared to answer questions but not to listen to comment, because it misleads the witness. He is leading me to give him the answers that suit him. He asked me a question, and I told him I was not the president of the National Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, Mr. Karadzic is charged with serious charges here and he's entitled to put any questions as long as it's relevant and related to his charges. The Chamber will monitor whether his questions are appropriate. So unless prohibited by the Chamber, I would like you to try to answer the question. And it is for the Chamber to monitor his cross-examination and then the Chamber will prohibit him from making any inappropriate comment. So unless indicated otherwise by the Chamber, please answer the question. Do you like the -- do you like the accused to repeat his last question, Mr. Redzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have stated, and we'll find where, that you were the president of the defence council in your municipality, and you told us today that the federal law and the federal constitution were no longer in force in Vlasenica from the moment when Croatia was attacked. Can you tell us when that happened according to whose decision and who decided the federal laws would be suspended?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: It's not true that anyone made that decision but it's true that there were talks were held in that town, talks to the effect that every problem in Yugoslavia has to be resolved by political negotiation, not by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, were those talks about Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. If you mean the negotiating team, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, let us try to shed light on the developments in Vlasenica, not what happened all over Yugoslavia, but never mind. Let's try to have this previous document admitted concerning the census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D1645, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I please ask Mr. Karadzic to give me transcript references or page references to the statement where he's saying that the witness is saying something. For example, you were president of the defence council in your municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll find it if you give me some time, because I did not expect the witness to go back on his own statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we've said that Milenko Stanic did not have direct jurisdiction over the national defence. There was a Secretary of National Defence who was under your jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The National Defence Council was a collective body, and it made decisions jointly. Neither Stanic or I had any control over it. It's a collective body that makes decisions based on a majority of votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago the Secretariat for National Defence. It's a part of the government, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a body of state administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have said, and that was in the statement of 12 October 1994, 65 ter 22597, on page 3, that Becir Mekanic who was probably president of the municipality before the multi-party elections was replaced and went back to his job in the national defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Mr. Mekanic a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was his position in the national defence? He came to the position of president of the Assembly from the national defence and went back to his former job.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: What happened before the multi-party system, it's normal that any citizen appointed to any position in the government retains his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We know that. We don't need to --

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: He was a desk officer in the national defence. You shouldn't be troubled about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do not overlap, and please put a pause between questions and answers. And, Mr. Karadzic, in particular to not start your question while his answers are being translated. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkovic was commander of the police station while the chief of the police station was this Milanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I cannot give an accurate answer, because I left Vlasenica earlier. I know that after the multi-party elections he was appointed commander of the Vlasenica police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. After the multi-party elections, the SDA and the SDS shared power. The chief of the public security station was a Serb, Milanovic, and as was customary, the number two spot belonged to the other ethnic community and that was the Muslims there and that was Fadil Turkovic over there; right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, for interrupting, but it's -- I'm just confused by the question and answer. "Q. Mr. Turkovic was commander of the police station while the chief of police station was this Milanovic; right?" "A. I cannot give an accurate answer because I left Vlasenica earlier. I know that after the multi-party elections he was appointed commander of the Vlasenica police station." I'm wondering if Mr. Karadzic can clarify who the "he" is because he talked about two gentlemen in the question and I don't know it's supposed to be Milanovic but Bjelanovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bjelanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Bjelanovic. Perhaps I did not articulate properly. Bjelanovic, a Serb, and then Fadil Turkovic was commander of the uniformed part of the police, commander of the armed police; right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The commander, yes, but it is the chief who holds all the keys in his hands, that is to say that the commander of the police cannot do anything without the approval of the chief of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in that very same statement on page 3 that they were appointed by the ministry, yes, the Ministry of the Interior; right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, that is something that both you and I know. So proposals are made by the municipality or, rather, the municipal organ or, rather, the SDS and the SDA and then it goes to federal level and the appropriate ministry gives its own consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also in the same place you said it wasn't the municipal authorities that could dismiss the chiefs of police, rather, the chief and the commander; right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: We, the municipal authorities could not operate that way, but the political parties could. It is the political parties, the ones that dismissed people and appointed their own people. We don't want to have a vacuum here. Let us understand each other properly. Every political party could propose its own people, of course, since they won the elections so it was the SDA and the SDS and then at state level it is the federal ministry that is in charge of actually giving consent and making the actual appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us clarify: The municipal level could provide proposals and as for changes in these appointments and dismissals, that was done by the ministry, right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: What is right is that the political parties were making the appointments. In this situation that we were living in municipal structures practically had no powers whatsoever. It was the political parties that made all these appointments and everyone knows how and in which way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, we have to be very specific. This is a criminal case. The political parties made proposals and the minister made appointments?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The federal minister as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic's comments are inappropriate. The witness was simply asking [sic] his question. If he doesn't like the answer, then that's not our problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, initially Mr. Karadzic's question didn't seem to be correct in light of the final question he posed. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also stated in that statement on page 4 that around the 27th of June, 1991, you became aware of the existence of irregular military units and that these irregular military units were something that you informed the national authorities in Sarajevo about; right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's true and even before that units were being established, materiel was being relocated and so on. You know that full well. You told your men where these vast amounts of weaponry were supposed to be relocated even in the spring of 1991 even before the aggression in Croatia or in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that I had powers over the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. You had reached a compromise with Milosevic and the military leadership. It was no longer a Yugoslav Army. It was cleansed of Catholics, Muslims, Macedonians, et cetera. It was basically 99 per cent Serb, and it was you, Karadzic, and your horrible units. You were in charge. And if we had weapons the way you did, there would never have been that kind of suffering because you are free only when you can display force against others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please let us focus on the facts. Do you have any proof of me having authority over the JNA, and if so, can you give this evidence to the Trial Chamber or the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, at the highest level of the SDS there were people who were in charge of talking to others and at a particular level. Your role and task was to talk to Milosevic and, of course, through him with the army as well. You're the one who is responsible, not only in view of the Bosniak Muslim people but also the Serb people and the Catholic people. You are responsible for everything that happened in Bosnia, you and your followers. You cannot excuse yourself from that. Your own people are going to damn you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, with all due respect, if you want me to be convicted leave political statements aside. Provide facts that prove what you are trying to say and what you feel about me. Give proof. But now let us go back to what you said on different occasions, and please respond to questions. Is it correct that before the war -- or, rather, that you said that before the war there was no open conflict between the Serbs and Muslims in the Executive Board of the municipality and parliament but there were conflicts among the people?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. That is not what I said. I said that there were no conflicts ever. Man, do you understand what I'm saying? People respected themselves to such a high degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I will need a week to examine you, Mr. Redzic, not only an hour and a half. Please look at your statement of the 12th of October, 1994. That is 65 ter 22597. On page 5, I'm going to read it out so that the translation is better than the one I provide. So I'm going to read it out in English. "[In English][Previous translation continues] ... Prior to the beginning of the war there were no open conflicts between the Muslims and Serbs in the Executive Council and the parliament, but there were conflicts between people." [Interpretation] Are you trying to say that the government functioned properly but that there were conflicts and tensions among the people?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. That is taken out of context. I was saying that there were individual clashes like anywhere in the world. Hoodlums can fight and so what, but that there was any kind of hatred on ethnic grounds I categorically reject that. And I'm not only talking about Vlasenica but all of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said on the same page, the same document, you said that you believed that Serb officials in the Assembly and in the SDS were secretly preparing a war. Is that what that you believed or is that something you have proof of?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: In view of what I know, the truth as you know yourself is that the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. I cannot --

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to give you five or six examples that will show that you were, indeed, preparing everything that happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You know about the decisions of the establishment of the Serbian Republic and also the instructions on the establishment of Serb municipalities and local communes of municipalities. You know alternatives A and B, the solutions at first and second level. All of that is what you and people who thought like you did. You know what the other documents were that you adopted and that you implemented. Are you trying to say that you don't know, you don't know what you did for the referendum? Do you know to what extent you indoctrinated the people so even those poor peasants the most honourable of people had to take up arms and fight against Muslims and Catholics? It is so ugly to be putting these questions today when the entire world knows what you did. May God forbid that you ever leave this courtroom otherwise who knows what will happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, please tell the Prosecution everything you know. Rest assured that they are going to use all of it if you have any such thing. Now let us deal with your statements. Let us see what your opinion is, what your feelings are, and what is your indubitable knowledge. Before this Court we need to see what your knowledge is that cannot be disputed or challenged. Please help us learn that. In this same statement on the same page 5 you said that people would confuse you with Stanic. Is it not correct that Stanic is considerably younger than you are, considerably taller than you are, and considerably lighter than you are?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is seven years younger and I repeat once again: We know that the rural area is rather illiterate both the Muslim and Serb areas and that indeed these people did come to municipal structures to complain about the distribution of weapons by the SDS to Serb members of that political party. That is the truth, and these people had never seen either Stanic or myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they came to see you to complain. Serbs complained against Serbs, and they came to see you. You claim that they came to you because they thought that you were Stanic and I claim that they came to you because they knew that you were a Muslim but you were simply in power and that they trusted you. Why are you ruling that out?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It's not their role to come and see a Muslim. Their role was to come to complain to the key man of the SDS, and they did not know that in a single room there was this secretary of mine and Mr. Stanic's. In view of everything that awaited us, all the problems that we were facing, don't you understand I told the secretary that if Stanic was not there she should direct everyone to see me, everyone who came there to that office, and that is how I found out what was happening in these villages that were 30 kilometres from the centre of Vlasenica. And sometimes some of these people would come to Vlasenica only twice a year, to the fair to sell their wheat and whatever else they produced. Don't you understand that, man?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to implore you, Mr. Redzic, just to answer my questions. We don't have time for all of this. We'll be here for a week. I'm going to put questions that require only a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you put the question that can be answered by yes or no, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you state that they complained to you that Izetbegovic's policy was to create a Muslim state and that Serbs would be killed if they cannot defend themselves? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: You should not take things out of context. It is true that I and Stanic visited Serb areas and that in conversations with people, Serbs, we asked why they had so many weapons. Even children, 15-year-old children had automatic weapons, and I said why did you have all of that? However, what they came to believe was that Alija would try to impose some kind of dzamahirija and there would be some Turks that would be killing them and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard of the Islamic Declaration?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of it, but perhaps you analyse it to a greater degree than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they protest with you against Bjelanovic who was not giving them any weapons?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, in general that's what they were saying, that it was only SDS members who were getting weapons and that they were not giving other Serbs weapons yet. I tried to pacify them and say that once the SDS members receive weapons they would be receiving weapons too. You understand that we were not little sheep, Radovan. We realised what was in the making. We realised that there would be a genocide. We needed to have basic things at least and we had to tell the republican government to tell the international community during negotiations that they should provide weapons so the people could defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you started arming the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, arming? No way. The Muslim people only had hunting guns that those who thought like you asked the people of Vlasenica to return and even that could not save their lives. They killed so many people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is for the learned Ms. Sutherland. Mr. Redzic said that he was president of the Council for National Defence in his statement of the 12th of October, 1994, on page 00148598 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, I'll have to think of some way to do this more efficiently. Are you saying that in Vlasenica there was no unit of the Patriotic League, the staff of the Patriotic League, the commander of that unit, that all of that did not exist and the Muslim community in Vlasenica was not armed illegally? Are you saying that or not?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I have to say the Patriotic League is absolutely not a military formation. Those are patriots from all communities and they would explain, explaining to Serbs and Muslims and Catholics and other faiths that Serb SDS was not telling the truth, that they will lead them to catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anyway there was an organisation of the Patriotic League in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, witness, that apart from Croatian municipalities in Western Herzegovina that would be the only municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina that would not have had a unit of the Patriotic League as early as September 1991?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I'm saying the Patriotic League is absolutely not a military organisation. It's a league of patriots that would try to dissuade the people from following you and falling for your deceit and deception. I would have known in my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we briefly see 1D4055. Do you see that this is a criminal report against Mustafa Zildzic, and it says that early in 1992, in January, February, March and April, he was in possession of an automatic weapon that the citizens were prohibited from acquiring at all, and he also had a large number of other weapons that he distributed amongst his neighbours. Did this man exist?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: If he did distribute weapons, I would be surprised to hear that he's still alive, because in those times, such people would have been liquidated. This man is alive, and he lives in Tuzla, and he works there. Where does this criminal report come from, from what sources? I don't know. I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The MUP reported this to the public prosecutor in May, and you see that he survived the Serbian police and the Serbian courts, Mr. Redzic. Although he not only had weapons in his personal possession, but he had an arsenal that he distributed to others.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, can this report be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder on what basis we can admit this. Did -- Mr. Redzic, did you know that this man distributed the weapons at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No way. In that time I was not in Vlasenica at all. This is dated 8 May 1992. I had left Vlasenica already, but I'm just saying that I doubt this, because this person would not be alive today if this document were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I just clarify that this was committed in the first months of 1991 when Mr. Redzic was in Vlasenica? You see the -- the passage in the box.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: And this is early 1992. What kind of report and what kind of charges are these? It's obvious that this document was prepared for somebody's defence. This report was made in 1992. It could have been done on New Year's Eve, Saint George's day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say this was forged for the purposes of my defence?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: You said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, can I hear you on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see anything about 1991 in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you see the page 1?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. 21 April 1992. It's written at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand 1991 either, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it's a matter of misinterpretation. I said early 1992, several months in early 1992. In legal language it's called unidentified dates, but it's a continuous activity. It's not a one-off thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. Your Honour, the witness, although, the witness said he wasn't aware of Mr. Turkovic distributing weapons in the early part of 1992 when he was in the municipality, it does go -- it does talk about events in the municipality at that period of time, so I leave it to Your Honours whether the document should be admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. On that basis we receive this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1646, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you noticed, Witness, that he received these weapons from Mr. Turkovic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this document. It looks suspicious to me. I don't know from which sources it could have been obtained. I would not like to comment, and it concerns a period when I had already left Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at 1D4056.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was going to ask Mr. Karadzic when the last document came up about the -- or the first document came up about the census. Where it's a lengthy document, if it's a four or five-page document could Mr. Karadzic tell the -- perhaps it might assist the witness if he knows the source of the document and the person that's actually the author of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very kind of you, Ms. Sutherland. I note the time, Mr. Karadzic. We'll have a break for 25 minutes, after which I would like you to plan your cross-examination in a more efficient way. Please bear in mind that you don't have to put everything to every witness. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, believe me, I'm not trying to attack you in any way. I'm just searching for the truth. You don't have to know everything, but it's important to me to know why, on what basis, you stated something. Let's deal with documents. 1D4056 is the document I would like to see next. Did the Party of Democratic Action deal with the issues of establishing the Muslim MUP?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. At that time, as far as the Muslims are concerned, the party did not play any role. They were state officials, and they acted in accordance with the constitution and the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the parties send anyone from Vlasenica to a training course in Croatia, a police course?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you look at this. I believe there's a translation. On 11 July 1991, Hasan Cengic, and somebody signed it on his behalf, Hasan Cengic is the acting secretary of the SDA, and he sent, to presidents of Executive Boards, this letter saying: "Hereby attached we are sending you a copy of a document about the admission procedure for candidates for the police force into the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this related to Vlasenica, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "To all presidents of Executive Boards." It says "copied to," and this is left blank for all municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness said he was President of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Vlasenica. He said he knows nothing about this document. There's no translation, and I don't think it should be admitted at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we not admitted similar documents that talk about these identical issues before, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a similar document, a similar instruction. This is just the cover letter, and what we had admitted before was an instruction listing the names of certain candidates. This is part of this entire drive by the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If this is just a cover letter of the document that has been admitted, that part can be admitted through a proper bar table motion. I don't think this is a proper witness to give foundation as to this document, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can do it that way too. Could we now see 1D4057.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Mirsad Srebrenikovic is?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No. That is not the surname that we encountered in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was in the ministry. He was a priest, a hodza, assistant minister for religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No way. I think it's inappropriate that organs infiltrated into municipal institutions deal with priests and religious affairs, that such people should occupy such important positions. I don't think it happened in the Vlasenica, in the republic or any other municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that Mirsad Srebrenikovic was not a hodza or that if he was, he was not assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that about the person you named. Perhaps through state authorities he was infiltrated to that position. I don't know if he ever occupied that position or how.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this, the list of candidates admitted to a training course for policemen. Let us see the next page now. You will see, Witness, that there are less than 10 per cent Serbs on this list, and you will see that there are candidates nominated from your municipality as well. We can leaf through the document. Do you see that it's 90 per cent Muslim, this force?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I'll tell you the exact number of Serbs on the police force in the active-duty police and the reserve police before the aggression. What you are stating are counter-indicators. In the reserve force of Vlasenica there were 80 per cent Serbs, between 70 and 80 per cent, and in the active force there were also 70 to 80 per cent Serbs. And then the tables were turned. I believe it was exactly the opposite. There were too many Serbs, disproportionately many to the actual ethnic composition of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we show him page 8 in B/C/S. There are two or three -- two candidates from Vlasenica. Do you by any chance know them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know them personally, but I know their last names, and they live at these addresses that are referred to; that is where these families live. However, I repeat once again: I don't know from which archives this material came and who compiled this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it can help you, Mr. Witness, it's from the Ministry of the Interior, the joint ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Show the first page. Show the witness the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "To all chiefs of public security stations, the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina," number such and such, the 12th of March, 1992. Telegram, telefax. It's their telex, actually.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't see a stamp. In our part of the world, in Bosnia, that is a sacred thing. There has to be a stamp. And I seem to have the impression that this is incorrect, incorrect indicators that you are showing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, a telex cannot be signed or stamped at that time.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: It can be seen. It can be stamped in one way or the other. This document is not binding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1647, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D4058. Can we have a look at that, please. Please, could you focus on this. This is the prosecutor's office in Vlasenica. It's a criminal report, number 1, Becir Mekanic, the person you mentioned. He was president of the municipality in the days of the Communists. Now, this is what he is being charged with. Number 5 is also a man from Vlasenica, Fadil Turkovic. Did you know Fadil Turkovic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we already talked about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was in the police, right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Commander of the Vlasenica police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just a moment. Please take a look at the date of this document. 1993, the 17th of June, 1993. The date itself associates all the previous actions taken and the intentions with which these actions were taken by certain parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at the next page to see what they're being charged with. You see what it says here? Because, due to, they killed five civilians in Rupovo Brdo. Do you know where Rupovo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I worked at the bauxite mine. It is only logical that I should know all of that. Now, whether they killed them, that is debatable. I cannot testify as to whether they had killed them or someone else or whether they were killed in fighting or something like that. I'm absolutely not going to say anything about that. It is not for me to say, especially not to speak about that particular point in time. I was far away in Tuzla and I was barley surviving.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, what do we do with this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have another opportunity to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D4059. Can we have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Behto Kahrimanovic, Kasim's son?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the Serbian version. Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 8th of June, 1991. So it was the joint Bosnia-Herzegovina. Kahrimanovic is giving a statement. He was a taxi driver in Vlasenica. He had done his military service. He's a Muslim, a citizen of the SFRY, and so on and so forth. And then further down what is encircled. It says four months ago the SUP of Zvornik took away two of my rifles and one pistol. Also the traffic police from Zvornik found in my car and took away 1.119 bullets, including 500 for small-calibre gun, 444 for a 7.62 millimetre gun and so on and so forth. And also in Holmec at the border crossing, four M-48 rifles were found by the customs officials that I bought in Austria with Amir Halilovic from Kula Grad in Zvornik. Can we have the next page now. You seek the encircled part here. It says: "I proposed to Sulejman that his wife come along as well so that we would be less conspicuous and of his own initiative he took his son. Sulejman's wife Hura knew what we were taking along. I believe that the child didn't know. The two of them were sitting in the back...," and so on and so forth. So it's your secretariat when you were in power in Vlasenica that took this statement. Are you trying to say that you did not know about this?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: We were never in power in Vlasenica, we, I mean. We were in power together with the Serbs and other ethnic communities. Now, whether the statement is correct and who took this statement, whoever took this statement was supposed to sign this and the appropriate organ was supposed to verify this. This has to do with a crime. Not in any remote backwater of the world would this kind of paper be valid. Invoking our own government, that defies common sense and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. I'm just asking you whether you knew that your secretariat, your police, that is part of the executive government that you headed, captured all of this and took this statement from the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this, but I claim once again that these are your versions, versions of yours and of people who think like you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? It's very important for the Defence what the witness does not know and what he should have known and what he should know and what he should be able to speak about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By now you have to know how to deal with the unfriendly, so to speak, unfriendly witnesses. You may call Mr. Kahrimanovic later on. There's no basis to admit this statement. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4060. Can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in June in the village of Hurici in your area weapons were being distributed, and do you know that your police compiled an official note about that?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I know the village of Sadici, the neighbouring village. Together with the president, I toured that village. I don't know anything who could have distribute used anything? Nothing, for heaven's sake, man, I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document from Vlasenica, the 17th of June. There is a signature of Milenko Sargic. There is a number, too. Who was Milenko Sargic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I think he was one of the inspectors there. He was a hardened member of the SDS and later on he proved to be the executor of your policy and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that information was collected to the effect that in the village of Sadici, the hamlet of Hurici, weapons were being distributed. And Muslims lived in Sadici or Hurici, you just mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Serbs and Muslims. Hurici is a hamlet inhabited by Muslims, yes, whereas Sadici includes Lazarevici and it's a mixed community anyway. The population is mixed Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1648, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4061.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Operation Oroz?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your municipality, your Secretariat of the Interior on the 24th of June, 1991. Basic plan of engagement in Operation Oroz and it says here that the security situation is complex in the republic and inter-ethnic and even inter-republican relations have been disrupted and that led to an increase in illegal weapons and ammunition trade. This station has information that confirms the assessment that the area of Vlasenica municipality is not immune to this sort of occurrence either and so on and so forth. And it also says that Behto Kahrimanovic from Kovacevici had weapons and ammunition seized from him. We saw his statement a moment ago. Can we have the next page please. Who was Mirhad Huremovic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: A person who worked in the MUP. Let me just say something. This report could only be compiled by the chief, that is, your man from the SDS. That could be seen very nicely. At that point the chief of MUP in Vlasenica, I mean at that time you hadn't divided Vlasenica. At that time you were not creating any sort of major problem because you were carrying out preparations. So it was your man who compiled this information so that it worked in your favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, well, my man said that your man should be in charge of the file on Operation Oroz and will be directly responsible for that and for collecting information about the distribution of weapons.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: That is inaccurate. Let us not try to persuade each other and let us tire the gentlemen here. It is incorrect. You were preparing for everything that would follow. Totally incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that there was no Operation Oroz and Radomir Bjelanovic, a Serb, did not appoint Mirhad Huremovic a Muslim as a person in charge of this operation of supervising what was going in terms of weapons smuggling?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: You should call Huremovic and ask him about that. They did not inform me about many other things either. They said that the MUP belonged to the republican MUP directly. I claim with full responsibility that this is incorrect. You should call Mr. Huremovic and he should give you his view whether this is truthful or not, or whether it's a forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have page 1 again. Is this a usual type of document in your municipality and could we find something like that in the registers there? You see here it has been registered. Could we please have the first page in Serbian. Is this the usual way of writing up an official document?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: One does know what an official document should look like. However, official documents can be forged, and you and your people were prepared to do anything if necessary to tear up everything that had to do with what happened over ten years and you could embark on such adventures. I wouldn't be surprised at any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of June, 2001, I wanted to tear up Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 26th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: A lot earlier. A lot earlier. You started these actions and operations aimed at tearing up Bosnia, because it was too small for you, 52.000 square kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1649, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D4109. Let us see how I was dividing up Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Adil Zulfikarpasic was?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Adil Zulfikarpasic was the president of the second-largest Muslim political party?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we do not have a translation. However, you have made me through your answer call up this document. Do you see Radovan Karadzic and Adil Zulfikarpasic at a panel discussion in Zvornik since this is written in Cyrillic the date is the 17th of August, 1991. Please help the Trial Chamber and tell them: Is that what is written here?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I know what you had in your heads, I assume, and the fact that you were misleading Zulfikarpasic or was Zulfikarpasic trying to prevent bloodshed in different ways also like other people who were in power from the SDA. In all sorts of ways we tried to avoid the bloodshed that you were planning with your followers. As for this here, I don't know. You probably didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's easy to prove all of that. You think that I got a hold of this old political --

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you do not pause before you start answering the question, interpreters find it very difficult to follow. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm also finding it difficult to follow. This wasn't on Mr. Karadzic's list that he provided at the beginning of this witness's cross-examination. He said then it was only because of the answer that the witness gave that he then called this document up. However, there's no translation, and I'm at a loss to actually know what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So I can give you no input whatsoever on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I found it difficult to follow that his answer made him call up this document now. But the last question was what? The last question and answer, both the question and the answers were not reflected in the transcript, because both of you overlapped and you spoke simply too fast. What was your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
